label: Corporate governance, risk and business continuity
description: The people who decide for a whole organization when something goes wrong: the board and its audit or risk committee, the executive team, general counsel and the disclosure committee, risk and compliance, and the business continuity manager. Three variants share one profile and differ in roles: a public company executive team and board (materiality, disclosure and board oversight), a business continuity and resilience program (functions, recovery time objectives and recovery order) and an academic case for business and law programs (roles, a facilitator and a scored debrief). Plans and doctrine: the crisis management plan and call tree, the disclosure controls and procedures, the business impact analysis, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 and the staff interpretations, the NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation, and the FFIEC business continuity booklet for banks. The company, its people, advisers and any ticker in an exercise are fictional. Exercise aid, not legal advice.

vocabulary.facility: the company (its head office, sites, systems and suppliers)
vocabulary.frontline: function owners, the business continuity team, the security team, the legal department and the finance close team
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the crisis management team room, the board portal and the disclosure committee

it: enterprise risk register and GRC platform
business impact analysis tool or spreadsheet
crisis management plan and call tree

roles.name: Board Chair / Lead Independent Director
roles.description: Convenes the board, approves extraordinary actions and decides what the board must hear and when.

roles.name: Audit or Risk Committee Chair
roles.description: Oversees cyber and continuity risk, receives incident reports and reviews disclosure.

roles.name: Chief Executive Officer
roles.description: Declares a crisis; approves a ransom decision, public statements and regulator contact; activates succession.

roles.name: Chief Financial Officer
roles.description: Owns the financial impact estimate for materiality, liquidity and insurance, and certifies filings.

roles.name: General Counsel
roles.description: Advises on materiality, directs outside counsel and forensics for privilege, drafts disclosure and issues the legal hold.

roles.name: Disclosure Committee Chair
roles.description: Runs the materiality determination process, drafts and approves the filing.

roles.name: Chief Information Security Officer
roles.description: Reports facts on scope and impact, escalates to the executive team and leads containment.

roles.name: Chief Risk Officer
roles.description: Holds risk appetite and impact tolerances and links the incident to the enterprise risk register.

roles.name: Chief Compliance Officer
roles.description: Tracks regulatory notice obligations and clocks and holds the regulator relationships.

roles.name: Internal Audit Head
roles.description: Gives an independent view of the response and later reviews the controls.

roles.name: Business Continuity Manager
roles.description: Activates continuity plans, owns the business impact analysis and tracks recovery against recovery time objectives.

roles.name: Chief Operating Officer / Function Owner
roles.description: Owns a critical function, reports its recovery status and decides recovery order with the BCM.

roles.name: Investor Relations / Chief Communications Officer
roles.description: Owns investor, analyst, employee and press messaging and keeps it consistent with the filing.

roles.name: Outside Counsel / Forensic Firm
roles.description: Runs the privileged investigation; advises on ransom negotiation and sanctions screening.

roles.name: Case Facilitator / Instructor
roles.description: Academic variant. Plays the outside world, sets the clock and leads the debrief.

outsideParties: outside counsel and the forensic firm
mediaChannels: the investor relations page and press releases
customer notices and the status page

sceneAnchors.control: a boardroom: a long table with water glasses and printed binders, a wall display showing a blank slide, leather chairs, a conference phone in the center

addedThreatFamilies.label: Cyber incident disclosure decision
addedThreatFamilies.description: Ransomware or data theft with extortion reaches the executive team; facts arrive in pieces and change, and the team must decide whether and when the incident is material, tell the board, and file with the SEC and other regulators on the clock.

phaseArc.title: Detection and first facts
phaseArc.goal: The CISO reports an incident with incomplete, partly wrong facts; the disclosure clock is not yet running but the duty to decide is.
beats: The CISO briefs the general counsel with scope still unknown
Outside counsel is engaged to direct the forensic firm so the work is privileged
A manager asks whether to wait for the full investigation before telling anyone senior

phaseArc.title: Scope and materiality determination
phaseArc.goal: Facts sharpen and the financial estimate becomes a range; the team must decide without waiting for certainty.
beats: The CFO gives an impact range that widens, then narrows
A committee member proposes to delay the meeting until Monday
Counsel reminds the team that investigation may continue after the determination
Time jump: the call is made, recorded and timed

phaseArc.title: Board, filing and notices
phaseArc.goal: The board is informed and approves the extraordinary steps; the filing, regulator notices and insurer notice go out in the right order.
beats: The board chair asks what directors need to see and when
A draft Item 1.05 filing and a press statement differ on the number of affected records
A regulator notice clock runs on a different trigger than the SEC clock
An Attorney General delay request arrives and the team must read what it does and does not change

phaseArc.title: Investors and review
phaseArc.goal: Investors, analysts, customers and employees react; the company keeps its messages consistent and reviews the decisions.
beats: An analyst call and the filing say different things
Employees get a message that contradicts the press release
A decision log review shows one decision with no recorded basis

decisionPointExamples: call the incident material now on the facts known, or wait a day for a firmer number and risk a call that looks delayed
file an Item 1.05 8-K, or an Item 8.01 8-K that does not claim materiality, and defend the choice
notify the full board tonight, or brief the audit committee chair first and the board in the morning
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a scope update from the CISO, a financial estimate range from the CFO, a counsel note on privilege, a staff interpretation that bears on the facts
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a facts update that reverses an earlier one, a director who cannot be reached, a forensic report not yet privileged, a filing agent cut-off
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: general counsel, the disclosure committee, the audit committee chair and outside counsel
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The company, its people, advisers, counterparties and any ticker are fictional. A draft carries the line 'Exercise aid, not legal advice.' Facts arrive late and change; early reports can be wrong. Never state that the investigation must finish before a materiality call. Item 1.05 drafts state the nature, scope and timing of the incident and its material or reasonably likely impact. Item 8.01 drafts do not claim materiality.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves materiality, disclosure, counsel, the board or a filing

addedThreatFamilies.label: Ransom payment decision
addedThreatFamilies.description: An extortion demand lands during an incident; the CEO, counsel, insurer and board weigh payment against alternatives, with sanctions screening, law enforcement contact and the disclosure duty that payment does not remove.

phaseArc.title: The demand
phaseArc.goal: A demand arrives with a deadline and a threat to publish data; the team first decides who may know and who decides.
beats: A ransom note carries a seven-day countdown
The insurer asks for notice before any contact with the actor
A director hears of the demand from the press

phaseArc.title: Options and screening
phaseArc.goal: Counsel, the insurer and the forensic firm lay out alternatives, restore options and the sanctions risk of paying.
beats: A negotiator reports the actor may be on a sanctions list
The BCM says restoring from backups would take longer than the business can bear
The CFO states a payment band against liquidity

phaseArc.title: The decision
phaseArc.goal: The CEO and board decide, and record who decided, on what information and what was considered.
beats: The board meets with counsel present to preserve privilege
A director dissents and asks that the dissent be recorded
Law enforcement asks for a short delay before any payment

phaseArc.title: After the decision
phaseArc.goal: Payment or not, the duty to decide on materiality and to notify regulators remains; the team documents the basis and tells regulators and the insurer.
beats: A regulator expects notice of an extortion payment within its own window
The decryption tool fails on part of the data
The post-incident review asks why the decision log lacks the sanctions step

decisionPointExamples: authorize a payment inside the insurer-approved band, or refuse and restore from backups for a longer outage
tell law enforcement before the negotiator makes first contact, or after
pay and treat the incident as closed, or recognize that payment does not end the duty to decide on materiality
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a sanctions screening result, an insurer coverage position, a negotiator proof-of-decryption test, a backup restore time estimate
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a payment platform that is closed over the weekend, a sanctions screening result still pending, a director conflict of interest, an actor who raises the price
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: outside counsel, the insurer and broker, law enforcement and the forensic firm
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The company, its people, advisers, counterparties and any ticker are fictional. A draft carries the line 'Exercise aid, not legal advice.' Never name a real ransomware group or a real wallet address. The sanctions screen and the insurer position are recorded in the decision paper before a payment decision. Payment size is one factor in materiality, and insurance reimbursement does not by itself make an incident immaterial.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves payment, sanctions screening, the insurer, counsel or law enforcement

addedThreatFamilies.label: Site or system loss against recovery objectives
addedThreatFamilies.description: A site, data center or key system is lost and the continuity team activates plans and tracks each critical function against its recovery time objective from the business impact analysis.

phaseArc.title: Loss and activation
phaseArc.goal: The loss is declared and the continuity plan is activated; the BCM and function owners decide scope.
beats: A fire, flood or power failure takes a site offline
The call tree reaches some managers and not others
A function owner asks to be recovered first

phaseArc.title: Recovery order
phaseArc.goal: Dependencies decide the recovery order; the BIA and the real dependencies disagree in one place.
beats: A payments function depends on a system ranked lower in the BIA
The alternate site has seats for half the staff
Time jump: four hours in, the tracker shows two functions past their RTO

phaseArc.title: Communications and obligations
phaseArc.goal: Customers, employees, regulators and the board learn of the outage; contractual and regulatory obligations start to bite.
beats: A key customer cites a service level clause
The board asks if the plan worked
A regulator asks about operational resilience

phaseArc.title: Return and review
phaseArc.goal: Functions return to normal; the team compares actual recovery with the objectives and decides what changes.
beats: Failback needs a data reconciliation nobody planned for
The review finds a function whose RTO was never realistic
The plan owner is asked to retest in ninety days

decisionPointExamples: recover the revenue function first, or the regulatory reporting function that has the nearer deadline
declare a disaster and move to the alternate site, or wait for a repair estimate
stretch an RTO with the customer, or invoke the contract and accept the dispute
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a dependency list from the BIA, a recovery estimate from IT, a backup restore test result, a supplier status notice
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a restore that takes twice the estimate, an alternate site with too few seats, a dependency missing from the BIA, a vendor that cannot be reached
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the business continuity manager, function owners, IT recovery and key customers
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The company, its people, advisers, counterparties and any ticker are fictional. A draft carries the line 'Exercise aid, not legal advice.' Each function has an RTO and a recovery point from the BIA; recovery claims are checked against elapsed exercise time. Status uses words (not started, in progress, recovered, past RTO).

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves recovery objectives, the continuity plan, an alternate site or function recovery

addedThreatFamilies.label: Supplier or cloud provider outage
addedThreatFamilies.description: A critical supplier, payment processor or cloud region fails; the company cannot fix it, so the work is dependency mapping, workarounds, customer commitments and what to tell the board and investors.

phaseArc.title: Outage and attribution
phaseArc.goal: The first signals are customer complaints; the provider status page is vague.
beats: Support tickets spike before the provider acknowledges anything
The provider status page says investigating
A function owner assumes the outage is internal

phaseArc.title: Dependency map
phaseArc.goal: The team finds which functions depend on the provider, including ones nobody listed.
beats: A finance close process turns out to use the same region
The BIA lists the provider but not its sub-provider
The contract has no right to audit

phaseArc.title: Workarounds and commitments
phaseArc.goal: Manual workarounds protect the most critical functions while customer and regulatory commitments are weighed.
beats: A manual process works at one tenth of normal volume
A customer asks for credit and a root-cause report
A regulator expects notice of a material third-party outage

phaseArc.title: Provider recovery and review
phaseArc.goal: The provider recovers; the company decides what to change about concentration and exit planning.
beats: The provider post-incident report differs from what the company saw
The board asks about concentration risk
Procurement is asked to price a second provider

decisionPointExamples: move critical workloads to a second provider mid-outage, or hold and wait for the first to recover
tell customers the cause is a supplier, or avoid naming it and risk a mismatch with the supplier statement
file a disclosure about a third-party outage, or document why it is not material
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a provider status update, a dependency list from procurement, a contract clause on service levels, a customer escalation
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a provider with no named contact, a workaround that needs credentials held by the provider, a second provider with no capacity, a contract exit clause with a long notice period
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the provider, key customers, procurement and the business continuity manager
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The company, its people, advisers, counterparties and any ticker are fictional. A draft carries the line 'Exercise aid, not legal advice.' The provider's own status page is the only source of its recovery time; do not invent a root cause the provider has not stated. Dependencies are named by function, system, supplier and site.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves the provider, a workaround, a contract or customer commitments

addedThreatFamilies.label: Executive succession and key-person loss
addedThreatFamilies.description: The CEO or CFO is suddenly unavailable; the board and the executive team work the chain of authority, delegations, signing power, disclosure duties and what to tell employees, investors and the press.

phaseArc.title: The event
phaseArc.goal: The board chair learns that an executive cannot serve; who knows and who decides is unclear.
beats: The news arrives through a family call, not a company channel
The general counsel asks what the bylaws say about interim authority
A banker asks who can now sign

phaseArc.title: Authority
phaseArc.goal: The board names an interim leader and confirms delegations; some documents still need a signature that nobody holds.
beats: The authority matrix is out of date
A wire needs two signatories and one is gone
An officer certification is due this week

phaseArc.title: Disclosure and messages
phaseArc.goal: The company decides what it must disclose and when, and keeps employee, customer and investor messages consistent.
beats: A Form 8-K item on a departure or appointment is considered
Employees hear from social media first
The press asks about health and counsel limits the answer

phaseArc.title: Stabilize and review
phaseArc.goal: The board confirms the permanent plan and reviews succession planning.
beats: A director proposes a permanent search
The audit committee asks about key-person insurance
The review finds the delegation list was never tested

decisionPointExamples: name an interim CEO tonight, or wait for the full board and risk a leadership gap
disclose the event now, or after confirming facts with the family and counsel
delegate signing authority narrowly to named officers, or broadly to keep operations moving
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a bylaw clause, an authority matrix row, a banking resolution, a counsel note on disclosure items
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a quorum problem, a signing authority nobody holds, a bank that wants a notarized resolution, a rumor ahead of the announcement
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the board chair, general counsel and the company bank
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The company, its people, advisers, counterparties and any ticker are fictional. A draft carries the line 'Exercise aid, not legal advice.' Health details of the fictional executive are never specific; the exercise concerns authority and disclosure, not the condition.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves authority, delegation, succession, the board or disclosure

addedThreatFamilies.label: Insider threat, deal leak or regulatory investigation
addedThreatFamilies.description: Confidential information escapes or a regulator asks for it: an insider copies sensitive files, a pending acquisition leaks, or a subpoena or inquiry arrives and the company must preserve documents and protect privilege.

phaseArc.title: Signal
phaseArc.goal: A leak, an unusual download or a regulator letter surfaces; the first decision is who needs to know.
beats: A reporter asks about a deal that only six people know
Security flags a large download by a departing employee
A subpoena summary reaches the general counsel on a Friday

phaseArc.title: Preserve and protect
phaseArc.goal: Counsel issues a legal hold and privilege reminder; the team decides how much to investigate before involving authorities.
beats: The IT team auto-deletes email after thirty days
A manager forwards a privileged memo to a vendor
An executive wants to confront the employee directly

phaseArc.title: Disclosure and obligations
phaseArc.goal: Securities, employment and regulatory duties meet: whether and how to disclose, who may trade, and what to tell a regulator.
beats: Trading is frozen for insiders
A selective disclosure question comes from an analyst
A regulator asks for documents within a short window

phaseArc.title: Resolve and review
phaseArc.goal: The matter is contained or escalated; the board hears the outcome and the lessons.
beats: The employee is separated and access is reviewed
The deal timeline moves
The audit committee asks whether controls would have caught it

decisionPointExamples: issue a legal hold now to a wide group, or narrow to avoid spreading the news
tell the deal counterparty about the leak, or hold until the facts are firm
cooperate fully and early with the regulator, or negotiate scope first
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a download log, a counsel note on privilege, a timeline of who knew the deal, a regulator letter with a response date
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: an auto-delete policy not yet suspended, a custodian on leave, a privileged document already forwarded, a deadline set before counsel can review
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: general counsel, outside counsel, human resources and the regulator
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The company, its people, advisers, counterparties and any ticker are fictional. A draft carries the line 'Exercise aid, not legal advice.' Names of employees, deals and regulators' staff are fictional. The exercise stays at the level of preservation, privilege, disclosure and governance decisions; it contains no technique for exfiltration.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves a legal hold, privilege, counsel, a regulator, trading or disclosure

noiseExamples: a shareholder asking about the dividend date
a vendor invoice query unrelated to the incident
a request to reschedule a routine committee meeting
a recruiter call for an executive
an employee question about benefits enrollment
pressureExamples: a filing agent cut-off at 5:30 p.m. Eastern
a director asking why they heard of it from the press
an analyst asking for a call before the market opens
an insurer asking for notice before any contact with the actor
a regulator giving a short response window
a key customer threatening to invoke a service level clause
